meta.note: Question bank authored against each module's own topics. `answer` is the 0-based index of the correct option. `why` is shown after answering, right or wrong.

0.q: Roughly how is study time split in this programme?
0.why: About 20% concepts, 20% video, 50% building and 10% assessment — the majority is hands-on.

options: Which version of your project is checked out
That Git is installed, and which release
The latest Git release available online
How many commits the repository has
0.why: It prints the installed client version, which is how you confirm the install worked.

0.q: Why must the course repository be public for GitHub Pages on a free account?
options: Pages cannot serve files at all from private repos on the free plan
0.why: Pages from a private repository needs a paid plan; on free, the repo must be public.

0.q: Which tool are you editing code in throughout this course?
0.why: VS Code, with Git and a browser alongside it.

0.q: What is the purpose of exporting your progress?
options: To back up your source code
To give the trainer a snapshot of what you have completed
0.why: It produces a dated JSON snapshot of modules, hours and videos for the trainer.

options: Encrypts traffic between browser and server
Translates a domain name into an IP address
1.why: DNS is the lookup layer: name in, address out. Encryption is TLS; storage is hosting.

1.q: A response arrives with status 301. What happened?
1.why: 301 is a permanent redirect. 404 is missing, 500 is a server error, 401/403 are auth.

1.q: Which DNS record type points a hostname at another hostname?
1.why: A maps to an IPv4 address; CNAME aliases one name to another. MX is mail, TXT is free text.

1.q: What is the practical difference between front-end and back-end?
options: Front-end runs in the browser, back-end runs on the server
Front-end is HTML, back-end is CSS
Front-end is free, back-end costs money
1.why: The split is about where the code executes, not which language it is written in.

1.q: What does HTTPS add over HTTP?
options: Encryption of the traffic in transit
Better SEO rankings and nothing else
1.why: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS — it encrypts and authenticates the connection.

1.q: Which DevTools panel shows you every request a page made?
1.why: The Network tab lists requests with status, size and timing.

2.q: Which tag correctly marks the main navigation of a page?
2.why: <nav> carries meaning for assistive technology; a div with a class carries none.

2.q: What is the `alt` attribute on an image for?
options: Text alternative for screen readers and when the image fails
The image caption shown below it
2.why: It is the text alternative — essential for accessibility, and shown if the image fails to load.

2.q: Which input type gives mobile users a numeric keypad and basic validation for an email address?
2.why: type="email" triggers the right keyboard and built-in format validation.

2.q: What does the `<label>` element do for a form field?
options: Associates descriptive text with the input, so clicking it focuses the field
2.why: A label tied to an input by `for`/`id` improves both usability and screen-reader output.
It must appear early in <head> so the browser decodes the document correctly.

2.q: When is a <table> the right element?
options: Whenever you need columns on a page
For laying out a page header
For genuinely tabular data with rows and columns of related values
2.why: Tables are for data. Page layout is Flexbox/Grid's job.

3.q: Which selector has the highest specificity?
3.why: An id beats classes, which beat element selectors. Ids are why !important fights start.
border-box folds padding and border into the declared width, which makes layouts predictable.

3.q: What is the difference between `rem` and `em`?
options: rem is relative to the root font size; em is relative to the element's own font size
em only works in media queries
3.why: em compounds through nesting; rem always resolves against the root, so it does not.

3.q: Where should CSS custom properties normally be declared for site-wide use?
options: On each element that uses them
3.why: :root makes them available document-wide and easy to override per theme.

options: It overrides the cascade, so the next override needs an even bigger hammer
It is not supported in modern browsers
3.why: It escalates specificity wars instead of resolving them. Fix the selector instead.

3.q: Which pseudo-class styles a link while the pointer is over it?
3.why: :hover is pointer-over; :active is during the click; :focus is keyboard/programmatic focus.

4.q: You need to lay out a row of items that wrap and share space along one axis. What fits best?
4.why: Flexbox is one-dimensional. Grid is for two-dimensional row-and-column layouts.

options: Columns at least 240px wide that fit as many as possible and share leftover space
4.why: It is the standard responsive grid idiom — no media query needed.

options: Base styles target small screens, then min-width media queries add complexity
Testing on a phone at the end
4.why: You start from the simplest layout and progressively enhance upward.

4.q: Which meta tag is required for responsive behaviour on phones?
4.why: Without it, mobile browsers render at a fake desktop width and zoom out.

4.q: Your page scrolls sideways on a 360px screen. What is the usual cause?
options: An element with a fixed width or overflow wider than the viewport
4.why: Hunt for fixed widths, long unbroken strings, or negative margins pushing past the viewport.

5.q: What is the difference between `let` and `const`?
options: const cannot be reassigned; let can
let is block-scoped, const is not
5.why: Both are block-scoped. const prevents reassignment of the binding (object contents can still change).

5.q: Which method returns the first element matching a CSS selector?
5.why: querySelector takes any CSS selector and returns the first match, or null.

5.q: What does `await` do inside an async function?
options: Pauses that function until the promise settles, without blocking the page
Converts a promise to a string
5.why: It suspends only that function; the rest of the page keeps running.

5.q: Which is the safe way to insert untrusted user text into the page?
5.why: textContent escapes the value. innerHTML would execute injected markup — that is XSS.

options: A new array of the same length with each item transformed
Only the items that pass a test
5.why: map transforms; filter selects; reduce collapses to one value.

5.q: `fetch()` resolved but the data is wrong. What should you check first?
5.why: fetch only rejects on network failure — a 404 or 500 still resolves, so check ok/status.

5.q: What does `event.preventDefault()` do on a form submit handler?
options: Stops the form's default page reload
5.why: It cancels the browser's built-in behaviour so your JavaScript can handle it.

options: Stages changes to be included in the next commit
6.why: add stages; commit records; push uploads. Three distinct steps.

6.q: Which command uploads your local commits to GitHub?
6.why: push sends commits to the remote; pull brings them down.

options: Secrets, .env files, node_modules and build output
6.why: Anything generated, huge, or secret. Committed keys must be rotated, not just deleted.

6.q: You committed an API key by mistake and then deleted it in a later commit. Are you safe?
options: Yes, the file no longer exists
No — it is still in history, so the key must be rotated
Yes, if the repo is private
6.why: History retains it. Treat the key as compromised and rotate it immediately.

6.q: Why should you avoid force-pushing a shared branch?
options: It rewrites history others have based work on
6.why: Rewriting shared history breaks everyone else's clone.

options: Two branches changed the same lines, so Git cannot decide automatically
A failed push due to permissions
6.why: Git marks the competing regions and asks a human to choose.

options: The browser tab the model runs in
The maximum amount of text the model can consider at once
How long the model has been trained
7.why: Everything — your prompt, files and the reply — must fit inside it.

options: They predict plausible continuations, and plausible is not the same as true
7.why: Fluency is not accuracy. Confident phrasing is not evidence of correctness.

7.q: A model confidently cites a library function. What should you do?
options: Use it, the model sounded certain
Check the official documentation before using it
Assume it is wrong and write everything yourself
7.why: Verify against the source of truth. This course exists partly because a report invented CLI commands.

7.q: Which of these should never be pasted into a public AI chat tool?
options: Client personal data, API keys or credentials
An error message from your own demo
7.why: Assume anything you paste may be retained. Secrets and personal data stay out.

7.q: Why might a model not know about a recent library version?
options: Its training data has a cutoff date
7.why: Training cutoffs mean current versions and APIs may be unknown or outdated.

8.q: Which prompt is most likely to produce usable code?
options: "Act as a front-end developer. Build a responsive pricing section in semantic HTML and CSS, mobile-first, no frameworks. Return one file."
8.why: Role, task, constraints and output format together remove the guesswork.

8.q: What are the six parts of the prompt structure taught here?
options: Who, what, when, where, why, how
Role, context, task, constraints, examples, acceptance criteria
Input, output, error, retry, log, done
Title, body, footer, header, style, script
8.why: Each part removes a category of ambiguity from the request.

8.q: The model returns broken code. What is the most effective next move?
options: Start a brand new chat and re-ask
Reply with the exact error text, the relevant file and the expected behaviour
Give up and write it manually
8.why: Specific evidence produces specific fixes. Vague complaints produce vague rewrites.

8.q: Why ask for a plan before asking for code?
options: You can correct the approach before a lot of code is written on a wrong foundation
It is required by the API
8.why: Reviewing a short plan is far cheaper than reviewing and unpicking hundreds of wrong lines.

8.q: What is a few-shot example in a prompt?
options: A sample input and desired output that demonstrates the pattern you want
8.why: Showing the shape of a good answer usually beats describing it.

9.q: You ask an assistant to review your code. What is the correct response to its suggestions?
options: Evaluate each one and apply only those you understand and agree with
9.why: A review is input, not instruction. Your rejection log is part of the module deliverable.

9.q: Which task is an AI assistant least reliable at?
options: Knowing the current version and API of a fast-moving library
9.why: Training cutoffs make current library specifics a classic failure mode.

9.q: A rejection log with zero rejections most likely means what?
options: You were not actually reviewing the output
9.why: Reviewing properly always turns up something to change.

9.q: What is the best way to use AI for requirements analysis?
options: Accept the generated feature list as final
Generate a first draft, then edit it with human judgement and note what you changed
Ask it to build the site immediately
9.why: It is a fast first draft, not a decision-maker.

9.q: Before using a generated component in production, you should:
options: Read it, test it in the browser, and check accessibility and responsiveness
9.why: Generated code is a starting point you are responsible for.

10.q: What is the practical benefit of a long context window for coding work?
options: You can supply several real files at once instead of describing them
10.why: Real code in context beats a summary of that code.

10.q: What is the point of a Project (persistent context) rather than a fresh chat each time?
options: Your brief and files stay available across conversations
10.why: Persistent context means you stop re-explaining the project every session.

10.q: You ask for a refactor of your own file. What should you do with the reply?
options: Paste it over the original immediately
Diff it against the original before accepting anything
Only read the first few lines
10.why: Diffing catches silently dropped behaviour — the most common refactor failure.

10.q: When is a reasoning-heavy model the right choice over a fast, cheap one?
options: For multi-step planning, architecture and tricky debugging
10.why: Match the model to the difficulty; simple mechanical work does not need the heavyweight.

10.q: What is the best way to give an assistant project context?
options: Upload or paste the actual files
Send a screenshot of the folder
Give it the repo name only
10.why: Actual source removes the guessing; a description of code is lossy.

11.q: How do you start an interactive Claude Code session?
11.why: Just `claude`. The source research for this course invented `claude plan`, `claude write`, `claude fix`, `claude test` and `claude doc` — none of those exist.

11.q: Which of these is NOT a real Claude Code command?
11.why: `claude fix` was fabricated by the source report. Real ones include mcp, doctor, update, config.

11.q: How do you run Claude Code non-interactively for a single prompt?
11.why: `-p` is print/headless mode, useful in scripts and pipelines.

options: Persistent project context the agent reads automatically
11.why: It is how you stop re-explaining conventions and structure every session. `/init` scaffolds one.

11.q: Why work on a branch when using an agent that edits files?
options: A bad change is easy to discard without touching main
11.why: Branch plus reading every diff before committing is the whole safety model.

11.q: What should you do with a large diff the agent produced?
options: Commit it if the app still runs
Trust it if there were no errors
11.why: "It runs" is not "it is correct". You are accountable for what you commit.

12.q: In the AI-assisted build cycle, why keep commits small?
options: A bad AI-generated change is easy to isolate and revert
12.why: Small commits make `git revert` a precision tool rather than a blunt one.

12.q: What is the correct order of the workflow taught here?
options: Plan (and edit the plan), scaffold, style, add behaviour, test, deploy
12.why: The plan is edited by a human before any code is generated.

12.q: Who is responsible for a bug in AI-generated code you shipped?
12.why: You committed it and you shipped it. That is the whole point of the review discipline.

12.q: What does the rejection log demonstrate?
options: That you exercised judgement rather than accepting output wholesale
12.why: It is evidence of review, which is the skill being assessed.

12.q: Before deploying, each AI-generated block should be:
12.why: Tidy-looking code fails just as often as messy code.

13.q: A REST call returns 200 but your code crashes reading the data. What is most likely?
options: The response shape is not what you assumed
13.why: 200 means the request succeeded, not that the body matches your expectation. Log it.

13.q: What does a CORS error actually mean?
options: Your code has a syntax error
The server did not authorise your origin to read the response
13.why: It is a browser-enforced policy decided by the server's headers — not a bug in your JavaScript.

13.q: Why can a paid API key never be safe in a GitHub Pages site?
options: Everything shipped to the browser is readable by anyone who opens DevTools
13.why: Static hosting has no server to hide a secret behind. Use a proxy or a key-less/public API.

13.q: What should a data-driven page show while a fetch is in flight?
options: A loading state, and an error state if it fails
13.why: Loading and error states are the difference between a demo and something usable.

13.q: Which HTTP method conventionally creates a new resource?
13.why: GET reads and should be side-effect free; POST submits data to create.

14.q: When does WordPress genuinely beat hand-coding?
options: When a non-technical client must edit content themselves
When the site is a single static page
14.why: The CMS earns its overhead when someone else needs to update content without a developer.

14.q: What is the biggest ongoing security risk on a WordPress site?
14.why: Unpatched plugins are the standard way small WordPress sites get compromised.

14.q: Before you hand a WordPress site to a client, you should have:
options: A tested backup and a written maintenance guide
14.why: A backup you have actually restored, plus documentation they can follow.

14.q: A backup you have never restored is best described as:
14.why: Restoring is the only thing that proves a backup works.

15.q: What does `useState` give a React component?
options: Local state that triggers a re-render when it changes
15.why: State plus re-render is the core idea; effects handle side effects like fetching.

15.q: When is vanilla JavaScript the better choice than React?
options: For a mostly static marketing or brochure site
15.why: A brochure site does not need a build step and a runtime to render text.

15.q: What are `key` props used for in a list?
options: Helping React identify which items changed between renders
15.why: Missing or index-based keys cause subtle bugs when the list reorders.

15.q: What does Next.js file-based routing mean?
options: You configure routes in a JSON file
The file structure in the app/pages directory defines the URLs
All routes go through one controller
15.why: The path on disk is the path in the URL.

16.q: Which file tells GitHub Pages to serve your custom domain?
16.why: A CNAME file in the published root, plus the matching DNS record at your registrar.

16.q: What does a `.nojekyll` file do on GitHub Pages?
options: Stops Jekyll processing, so files and folders starting with _ are served as-is
16.why: Without it, Jekyll can silently skip files whose names begin with an underscore.

16.q: Lighthouse reports a poor LCP. What is the usual first thing to check?
options: The largest above-the-fold image or render-blocking resource
16.why: LCP is usually dominated by a hero image or blocking CSS/fonts.

16.q: How do you undo a bad deploy on GitHub Pages?
options: Revert the commit and push — Pages rebuilds from the branch
16.why: The published site follows the branch, so `git revert` plus push is the rollback.

16.q: Why enforce HTTPS on your Pages site?
options: It encrypts traffic and is required for many browser APIs
16.why: Security, plus modern browser features that refuse to run on insecure origins.

17.q: What is a canonical URL for?
options: Telling search engines which URL is the authoritative version of duplicate content
17.why: It consolidates ranking signals when the same content is reachable at several URLs.

17.q: Which Core Web Vital measures visual stability?
17.why: CLS is Cumulative Layout Shift — content jumping as the page loads.

17.q: How many <h1> elements should a typical page have?
options: One, describing the page's main subject
17.why: A single clear h1 with a sensible heading hierarchy beneath it.

options: Guarantees pages stay out of search results
Advises crawlers which paths they should not crawl
17.why: It is guidance for crawling, not a security control and not a reliable way to hide a page.

17.q: Which accessibility check can you do in under a minute with no tools?
options: Navigate the whole page using only the keyboard
17.why: If you cannot reach or see focus on a control, neither can a keyboard user.

18.q: What makes this line dangerous: `el.innerHTML = userInput`?
options: Injected markup and scripts in the input will execute — that is XSS
18.why: Use textContent for untrusted text, or sanitise deliberately if markup is genuinely required.

18.q: You accidentally pushed an API key to GitHub. What is the first step?
18.why: Assume it was scraped within seconds. Rotation is the only thing that actually helps.

18.q: Where should secrets live for a project with a build step?
18.why: And remember front-end bundles are public — server-side is the only place a secret stays secret.

options: Known published vulnerabilities in your dependency tree
18.why: It checks installed versions against a vulnerability database.

18.q: Why is HTTPS a security control and not just a ranking tweak?
options: It prevents tampering and eavesdropping on traffic in transit
18.why: It protects the connection. It does not protect against XSS or a compromised server.

20.q: DNS resolves a name to what?
20.why: Name to address. That is the whole job.

20.q: Which Git command stages a change for the next commit?
20.why: add stages, commit records, push uploads.

20.q: Which selector wins: `#nav a` or `.menu a.active`?
options: Whichever is last in the file
20.why: One id outranks any number of classes.

options: No — it resolves, so you must check response.ok
20.why: fetch rejects on network failure only. HTTP error statuses still resolve.

20.q: Which is a real Claude Code command?
20.why: doctor is real; write, test and doc were fabricated by this course's source research.

20.q: What is the safest way to render untrusted text?
20.why: textContent escapes it. innerHTML is the classic XSS vector.

20.q: A committed secret is fixed by:
20.why: History keeps it. Only rotation removes the risk.

20.q: Mobile-first means base styles target which screen?
options: Small screens, enhanced upward with min-width queries
20.why: Start simple, add complexity as space allows.

20.q: Why must you verify AI-generated code against documentation?
options: Models can state non-existent APIs with complete confidence
20.why: This curriculum's source report invented five Claude Code commands. Confidence is not correctness.

20.q: Which CSS property makes width include padding and border?
20.why: border-box is what makes widths behave the way most people expect.
